title: An ordinary night
hookLine: Fatima asks her father for a servant; he comes at bedtime with words instead
tomorrow: why does a box of spices come out when the day of rest ends?

lines: FATIMA'S HANDS, SORE FROM THE MILL.
cards: What are the last words you say before sleep? Sometimes they're to a screen. In Medina, Fatima, the daughter of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, had sore hands from grinding grain on a hand mill.
She heard her father had received captives who could work as servants, so she went to ask for one. He wasn't home. That night he came to her house after she and her husband Ali had gone to bed.
They started to get up. Stay where you are, he said, and he sat down between them.

teach.b: He didn't bring a servant. He brought words. Shall I not teach you something better than what you asked?

When you go to bed, say Allahu akbar, God is greatest, thirty-four times; subhan Allah, glory be to God, thirty-three; alhamdulillah, praise be to God, thirty-three. That is better for you than a servant.
The story is in Sahih al-Bukhari, and those bedtime words are known as the tasbih of Fatima. Now the debate, because readers hear this story in two ways.

teach.h: READING ONE: A NO, FOR FAIRNESS.
teach.b: One reading hears a no, for fairness. In another telling, in the collection of Imam Ahmad, he says he can't give to them while the poor around him go hungry.
His own family doesn't jump the line, and the words are what he can give.

teach.h: READING TWO: THE WORDS ARE THE HELP.
teach.b: The other reading hears a better yes: the words are the help. Said at night, they turn a tired body toward God, and the strength for tomorrow's grinding comes from there. Each side has a best case.

The first: a good no protects someone you can't see. The second: some help doesn't take the work away; it changes how you carry it. Either way the night ends in the same place, not on the complaint, but on praise.

how: Muslims who keep the tasbih of Fatima say it at bedtime, as the hadith gives it: Allahu akbar thirty-four times, subhan Allah and alhamdulillah thirty-three times each, counted on the fingers or on prayer beads.

o: a short message wishing someone sweet dreams
the words you end the day with before sleep
the hour when the house finally goes quiet

games.q: the night words: tap the pairs.
p: asked for a servant; her hands hurt
sat between them and gave words

s: the Prophet sent Fatima a servant the next day
in Bukhari's telling he gave words instead: better for you than a servant.
the words are given for bedtime
that's how the hadith gives them: when you go to bed.
Muslims read the story only one way
some hear a no for fairness; others hear the words themselves as the help.

games.q: a friend says the Prophet simply turned his daughter down. you hear a gift. what's the best case for her side?
o: a fair no: in Ahmad's telling, others were hungry, so his family didn't go first.
he didn't mind that her hands hurt; hard work was meant to stay hard.
servants weren't allowed in Medina, so he couldn't have helped anyway.
games.why: the strongest 'no' reading is about fairness: in one telling he won't give to them while others go hungry. the 'gift' reading says the words are the help.

practice: The tasbih of Fatima is counted on the fingers, so borrow the counting. Touch your thumb to each fingertip in turn, one slow breath for each, and keep going around your hand until the bell.
Anyone who keeps the tasbih can say Fatima's words on the same fingers.

wordCard.voice: An ordinary night: the last minutes before sleep, and the words you choose to end them with.

orig.note: Arabic: glory be to God, one of the three phrases the Prophet gave Fatima for bedtime (Sahih al-Bukhari 3705).

carryVoice: Pocket this one: goodnight can be a gift, words handed over at the edge of sleep. Rest easy.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3705 (also 5361, 6318): Fatima asks for a servant; the Prophet comes at bedtime and teaches takbir 34, tasbih 33, tahmid 33, 'better for you than a servant'
Musnad Ahmad (the telling in which he will not give to them while the poor go hungry)
